items.body: Review by Steve Conrad — An Apocalyptic COVID-Confectionary ConstructionApocalyptic: "Relating to or predicting widespread destruction or the collapse of civilization." (American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language).I mean, look at this cover art- it positions the Rock Boutique as the last outpost of...something...before one ventures into the apocalyptic wilderness- the Elon Musk-esque rocket ship preparing to exit the planet (whichever planet this may be), the more-angular St. Louis arch, the slightly blood-shot mechanical eye in full surveillance mode, and the almost confectionary-appearing glowing purple...objects, which are (menacingly?) beginning to multiply within Morri's domain.And the "wheel in the sky"- biblical Ezekiel reference- and yes, what the heck is that reference? While the stream (with fiery twinkles) wends its way through the landscape.The COVID-ConfectionSo, on this third album from Chicago, USA's "progressive rock collective, REFESTRAMUS, the stage is set for the seven (on Bandcamp, nine) tracks featured on "Morri's Rock Boutique).I'm hearing these tracks- whichever version of the album you choose- as "COVID-Confection" since according to the band's bio- drummer/songwriter/lyricist Derek Ferguson formed the first incarnation of REFESTRAMUS during the initial onslaught of the worldwide global scourge of COVID, and the music on this album at least for me- an early progressive rock geek- reeks of the sort of touches that made Styx a lot of money, as well as the grandeur and flourishes that endeared many of us folks-of-a-certain-age to the progressive genre.I remember a faintly condescending review (probably in Rolling Stone, which in those days was holy writ for me) of one of the 70's era KANSAS albums, in which the all-knowing reviewer said something like, "it's fairly decent music, but with wedding-cake arrangements". Little did this reviewer know that these "wedding cake" arrangements were exactly what made some of us geeks sit up and pay attention!Which is to say that on this album, where are many "confectionary" sections that delight an aging geek, and might delight you as well, regardless of your age and geekiness. Keyboardist/vocalist Dyanne Potter Vogetlin provides standout synth and keyboard fills and flourishes that genuinely soar, that color the overall sound with richness and verve. One can hear this almost from the very beginning of the album.To this reviewer, the bass guitar and vocal prowess of Jan Christiana are almost other-worldly. Upon first hearing, I wondered who on earth could actually sing that high, with that kind of power and control? Well, Jan can. I suspect Jan also has a lot to do with the vocal arrangements, which are lush and varied, and become an additional "unsung" instrument in the confectionary construction of "Morri's Rock Boutique".So yes, even on the opening "Storms" and then certainly on the (Russian folk tale-based) "The Cossack's Dream", we get the kind of grandeur and sweep of early era progressive and glam-rock music. I had to think of AVIARY and of course Styx, sometimes even Queen due to the vocal flourishes.None of this is to diminish or minimize the contributions of each musician- it is a "rock collective" of accomplished musicians who play supremely well together, and given a spacious production by Ian Beaubout. The variety of approaches on this album is also worth mentioning, including the Russian, and later the Asian touches complete with instrumentation like shamisen, koto, and shakuhachi found on "Lakeview Samurai"- engagingly sung by Nam Chumo.Lakeview Samurai appeals to me like confection- surface sweetness, not so much substance. I can get the references to some of the current cultural scene, and the side-by-side transposition of the ancient and venerable samurai code. Everything is done well, it simply doesn't touch me very deeply, nor perhaps, fit within the framework of this album.Same goes for "Hell or NYC", pointing out the stereotypes (and perhaps well-deserved) of the coldness and rudeness of the vast population of that enormous and varied city. The sax touches and the film-noir story-telling is captivating- yet still, confection, for better or worse.I guess the themes being explored allow different interpretations- for me, the overall affect of the collection of tracks is that it seems like "pastiche", rather than coherent whole- in the sense of the "hodgepodge" definition of pastiche. And maybe that's Derek's point and his intention.In ConclusionIt's excellently done, catchy, filled with verve and variety, demonstrating fine musicianship from each participant in this production- progressive rock luminaries and newcomers too. AND at the same time, for better or worse, confectionary. I'm going with 3.5 candied stars, but rounding up to 4 thanks to the overall fine effort given.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Cornwall's anachronistic Arthurian spacemen return with their seventh full-length studio album release since their formation (in Edinburgh) in 2010 and second in two years (which is unusually fast for them). 1. "Song of the Rainforest" (21:20) a vocal-less and more keyboard-generated epic than the usual Emerald Dawn offerings. Also, it feels as if the presence and contributions of Dave Greenaway and Tom Jackson here are on the same level of importance (and dynamics) as those of Ally and Tree. (36/40)- i. "Balance" - after a long 90-second intro of cave dripping sounds and two alternating sustained organ chords slowly establishing their pace and fullness and then the entrance and establishment of bass and drums into an awesome funk-lite vamp groove of two gorgeous Mellotron-like chords Ally enters with his seering electric guitar to deliver one of his best guitar solos ever--for five minutes! The contagious groove established by Dave Greenaway and Tom Jackson is awesome. - ii. Incursions - a stop-and-pause precedes a very slow switch to Smooth Reggae groove over which Ally solos with his tenor sax. As Trees synth strings enter (and Ally's tenor sax desists), the beat is sped up (we're now into the ninth minute), which prompts Ally to switch to his soprano sax--which gives Tree a little more room and license to embellish with her variety of synth strings riffs: often matching or meeting Ally's sax lines with her own.- iii. "Loss" - in the 11th minute another interlude of synth strings intervals paves the way for a heavier, almost ominous motif to set up with Tom's more tribalistic tom-tom-centered (synthetic talking drum?) drumming and Dave's heavily-wowed bass play being stomped over by some deep monster-saw keyboard and guitar riffs. The keyboards continue riffing--kind of soloing--for a couple of minutes over this motif before . . . - iv. "Regret" - the 14th minute has the establishment of a peaceful, perhaps sad motif of jungle/tropical sounds (including Tree's Amazonian flute) woven loosely around one another until the 18th minute when saw synth chords take over and Ally returns to shredding emotionally on his guitar. One of the most evocative, sensitive, and surprisingly tight--even thoughtful--sections of any Emerald Dawn song I've ever encountered. 2. "Rivers of Tears" (14:58) opens with a jaunty journey of jazz-classical-sounding solo piano play. Among the most impressive and pretty keyboard play I've ever heard from Tree! At 1:40 bass, drums, and, eventually, Ally's "reverberated-into-the-background" electric guitar slowly enter. Tree continues to tinkle the ivories within and behind the guitar, bass, and drums while adding some washes of synth strings to the mix as Ally continues shredding (as he does). Then Ally stops, making room for Tree to expand her piano note play as Tom and Dave slowly, gradually slow down and drop out. a pause/break at 3:30 results in the unleashing of Tree's reverb-drenched voice over only the banks of synth strings chords and still tinkling piano note play (mostly in progressing arpeggios)--which eventually becomes just synth strings as we enter into another little pause around 5:30. Here Tree establishes a chord progression with the repetition of four descending arpeggiated chords over which the rhythm section joins in and Ally deploys his tenor sax. Another pause at the seven-minute mark leads into a transference of the play of the descending chord pattern to synth strings as Tom and Dave kick back and Ally switches to electric guitar. Here Dave's bass playing is a bit rote and uninventive while the embellishments that Tom adds to his drumming feel a bit forced and "required" while Ally's guitar shredding sounds/feels . . . the same as ever. A little pause at the end of the tenth minute is filled with Tree's vocal lines until the band re-emerges with a kind of two-chord "tropical" vamp. Yet another stop and transition at 11:45 as the band shifts into a much more dark and ominous section--launched off as Tree shouts out a "Poison. Into. It's veins." declaration. This section could almost be coming from NIL or KING CRIMSON--even with Tree's operatic high-note repeat delivery of the word "poison." The motif then morphs in the second half of the 14th minute into something more akin to a Led Zeppelin descending chord progression--which it plays out to the song's end with embellishing accents coming from Ally's synths and Tom's drums. Not bad! (26.375/30)- i. "The Natural Cycle" - ii. "Disruption" 3. "Paradise" (8:56) opening with some excitingly pregnant synthesizer play--chords, bass, and peppy upper register riffs--which subside when Tree's plaintive, melancholy voice enters at 0:33 to introduce the song's theme. By the one minute mark she pauses wherein Tom and Mark enter with a cool, jazzy, STING "Englishman in New York"-like motif (which then happens to support Tree's "Englishman in New York" vocal melody lines). Nice bass line beneath Tree's organ chords as Ally enters with a bluesier Gilmour-like approach to his injections of guitar riffs and flurries. Around the four-minute mark the band slows things down, Tree's voice softens, while Mark and Tom's play kind of moves into greater prominence as Ally and Tree's keyboard play slides more into the background of the mix. Interesting! And I like it: I like having the bass and drums mixed in front of the keys, guitars, and saxes. The synth strings and guitar soloing in the next two minutes feel much more like the sound palette of Polish NeoProg masters COLLAGE's great textures on their Moonshine masterpiece (especially "The Blues"). In the seventh minute one of the keys begins to repeat and develop a melody line from THE MOODY BLUES' "Nights in White Satin," to which Tom backs down for a bit, but then everybody ramps up again into a fully-COLLAGE motif in which the synth strings continue soloing as other synth chords continue to deploy the "Nights in White Satin" chords and melody-reminders. Brilliant! And this is how they choose to end the song, the album! Awesome! Despite the "borrowing" of the sound palette and melody/chords, I finally feel as if The Emerald Dawn have arrived to the gates of top-tier prog, the symphonic side! (18.75/20)- i. "Losing Paradise"- ii. "Harmony Regained"Total Time 45:14I like the more sophisticated complexities ED are injecting into their compositions as it diminishes the dreaded monotony wrought of their old style of endlessly jamming over simple and often drawn-out single- and/or double-chorded vamps. Either their music theory has improved or they've decided to let go of the stoner-rock approach to song-rendering and employ more symphonic structuring for their music--whatever it is, I like it!A-/4.5 stars; a stunningly-improved advancement of compositional design yields the best album of The Emerald Dawn's career--one that has them knocking on the door of the Valhalla of the Symphonic Prog masters! I'm bumping up this rating into masterpiece status for the surprising display of growth as well as this being, in my opinion, Emerald Dawn's best album yet.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 982Le Orme is one of the longest lasting and best known Italian progressive rock bands. Le Orme was formed in Venice in 1966 by Aldo Tagliapietra (voice and guitars), Nino Smeraldi (guitars), Claudio Galietti (guitar and bass) and Marino Rebeschini (drums). Their first album, "Ad Gloriam" was released in 1968. From their psychedelic and beat initial roots, the band moved into much more increasingly sophisticated musical structures. In that line, the band released two excellent albums "Collage" in 1971 and "Uomo Di Pezza" in the following year. Their 1973 album "Felona E Sorona" is widely regarded as one of the top albums in the Italian progressive rock scene. By this time, the band consisted of Tagliapietra (mostly on bass with some guitar) along with keyboard player Tony Pagliuca and drummer Michi Dei Rossi."Felona E Sorona - Deluxe Edition (English And Italian Versions)" is a very special compilation album of Le Orme that was released in 2011. This is an economic package that includes their fourth studio album "Felona E Sorona", released in 1973, in its original Italian version, and their fifth studio album, which is the same album but in its English version and that was also released in the same year. This can be a very interesting compilation album because it includes the two versions of the album. As many of us know, "Felona E Sorona" is in general considered the best work from the band and is also considered a landmark to Italian progressive rock as one of the best and most important progressive rock albums ever made, especially in the Italian progressive rock scene. So, what we have really here is a great album in its two versions, probably at a cheaper price, and what will be a very worthwhile purchase, especially for those who are collectors and huge fans of Le Orme, fans of the Italian progressive rock or fans of the great prog music in general.As I'm going to review these two albums on Progarchives, in a more extensive way, I'm not going to do it at this moment. So, if you are interested to know, in more detail, what I'll write about them later, I invite you to read both of my reviews, in time. However, here I'm going to write something about them in a shorter way. So, of course, I'm not going to analyze them track by track, as I'm going to do, but I'm only going to make a global appreciation of both albums."Felona E Sorona" - Italian Version: "Felona E Sorona" is one of the classic albums of the Italian prog rock scene. The album quickly reached the top of the Italian charts giving the band their second gold record. Like many others, I find "Felona E Sorona" to be Le Orme's most fascinating work. In less than 35 minutes, Le Orme delivers probably their greatest masterpiece. Their high level of musicianship is evident over the all album. The focus is more on mood, song structure, and texture. As a concept work and despite the nine pieces, mostly short pieces and with a lot of variety, the album sounds very homogeneous and less like a collection of individual songs. This is an album that still has a strong influence in the world of progressive rock to the point that La Maschera Di Cera paid tribute to it by extending its theme and even going so far as to take up and transform the superb original cover. "Felona E Sorona" is a true classic of the movement and it's unforgivable not to have it if you like Italian prog rock. "Felona E Sorona" is an absolute must-buy."Felona E Sorona" - English Version: "Felona E Sorona" is a beautiful album, soaked with that 70's flavour that we all prog rock fans love. Although it's by no means technical, the band presents a unique sound that combines vocal parts that exude a unique sense of song with dramatic instrumental parts that make full use of synths and organs to portray a variety of scenes, including lyricism and thrills. It's an album of the golden years of progressive. Like their compatriots Premiata Forneria Marconi and Banco Del Mutuo Soccorso, "Felona E Sorona" was also released in the original Italian version and in the English version. At the request of Tony Stratton-Smith the owner of Charisma Records, Le Orme recorded an English version of the album with lyrics translated by Peter Hammill. It was also entitled "Felona E Sorona" and was also released in 1973. The English album is very similar, except that the vocals were more expressive and appropriate in Italian. This English version is also very good but listen to the Italian version because it's much better.Conclusion: Italian and English versions of the album give the listener the opportunity to hear the English lyrics, and yet enjoy the authentic feel of the original album. Well written notes in both Italian and English, including song lyrics. The essay in these notes gave me a proper understanding of what this album is about, as well as details about the album's production. As a bonus, there are also some band photos and copies of original mixes and vinyl stickers, both English and Italian. However, there's a poor sound quality for the English version. The volume is lower than that of the Italian version, which is a pity. Besides, I strongly prefer the Italian vocals to the English. I think escape to us some of the most important parts of the original album, which are the vocals. I can understand why many people, especially the non-Latin language speakers, prefer the English version. But, definitely, the original is always better than the copy.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: I’m dying In your Subterranean World Geranium eye Kiss of the poison flower There are dreams in which we run from monsters, and others in which the monster is time itself. You move through a room of people arrested between gestures, mouths open around unfinished words, hands suspended above tables, faces fixed by some invisible Mombi whose spell has spared only you. At first, there is curiosity. Then comes the dreadful privilege of observation. You notice how strange a human being becomes when deprived of motion, how life resides in the smallest continuation. And as you weave among them, one thought follows closely behind: perhaps they are not frozen. Perhaps you are passing. Los Angeles artist Blone Noble has spent 2026 behaving as though settling on one particular musical identity might constitute a misdemeanor. After May’s Dominator EP pushed New Beat, industrial, and Italo into the club, the eerie Subterranean World, co-written and produced by Dakota Blue, takes the stranger route: down the trapdoor, past the plumbing, and into an underworld where romance has acquired pincers. Noble describes the collaboration, though the music suggests dangerous laboratory conditions: “Dakota Blue and I have been working in the shadows for some time now, developing a new musical language in his Pasadena studio; a neo-futuristic art rock record built on primal rhythms, eastern synths, fretless wanderings and LA noir poetry. We wrote and recorded Subterranean World in our first session together.” That Mick Karn fixation makes itself known through Blue’s fretless bass, which prowls rather than anchors, carrying echoes of Dali’s Car, Japan, Bryan Ferry’s Bête Noire, and Talk Talk’s The Colour Of Spring without turning the song into a museum tour. Noble’s droning vocal inhabits the music with the calm of somebody describing his poisoning while deciding the flowers were worth it. The lyrics take erotic obsession underground, where devotion means accepting humiliation, death, poverty, insects, occult initiation, and whatever other indignities love has stored in the basement. Romance has rarely sounded so eager to be eaten alive. Director Redamo Rosa gives that delirium an unnerving visual form. His camera passes through bizarre tableaux populated by people frozen, as though Medusa had wandered through a Twilight Zone episode and decided everyone needed to hold still for continuity. Bodies become mannequins, gestures hang unfinished, and rooms acquire the logic of a bad dream you understand until breakfast. “I had this idea to have a camera move through dreams, almost like walking through a museum or diorama of a reality, only this reality is slightly bent,” Rosa explains. “I didn’t want there to be any reason behind the visuals, but I wanted the audience to feel disoriented by what they’re seeing. Often, we find deep meaning in inexplicable dreams. I approached Blone Noble with the idea, and he played Subterranean World for me. The song captured that feeling I was chasing – it played like narration to a nightmare and felt like it was about the darkest parts of humanity.” The result feels deliciously wrong, a surreal dip in the darkest shadows of our psyches, where everybody else has stopped moving and the camera, cursed with consciousness, keeps going. Watch the video for Subterranean World below: Listen to Subterranean World below and purchase the single here. items.body: Dutch post-punk project Bragolin has cast a looming shadow across the international darkwave scene. For the past eight years, its music has passed from listener to listener through word of mouth and digital playlists assembled with the care once given to hand-dubbed mixtapes. With about 300,000 monthly Spotify listeners, the band now stands among the Netherlands’ most-listened-to contemporary wave exports, drawing an audience far beyond Utrecht. The band began there in 2013, when Edwin van der Velde transferred a guitar riff intended for his Dutch-language project Zwarte Poëzie onto a newly purchased Bass VI. The instrument changed the riff’s character and, with it, the course of his work. That piece became Into Those Woods, the first Bragolin song and a centerpiece of the 2018 debut, I Saw Nothing Good So I Left. The album has since been repressed six times on vinyl, while the track’s baritone hook carried it beyond ten million streams and onto darkwave dance floors around the world. Van der Velde expanded Bragolin in 2019 through Let Out The Noise Inside, a full-album collaboration with Adam Tristar that brought more electronic production into the project. Synth player Edwin Daatselaar joined the following year, establishing the current live duo; both musicians also play in Zwarte Poëzie. Bragolin has since performed more than one hundred shows across Europe and Latin America, including appearances at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Amphi Festival, Cold Hearted Festival, Extramuralhas, and Kalabalik. The debut has continued to find new listeners as well: seven years after its release, This Grotesque Dance took off on TikTok and is now Bragolin’s most-streamed song, with over 7 million streams on Spotify alone. Bragolin’s third album, I Don’t Like What It Does to Me, retains the Bass VI, organ tones, and dance rhythms at the center of van der Velde’s writing while widening the arrangements with waterphone, synthetic ocean textures, seagull field recordings, strings, and a guitarless piece assembled entirely from layered Clavinets. “Visuals are what draw my attention,” van der Velde says, and references to The Lighthouse, It Follows, The Thing, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers enter these songs as stories of pursuit, artificial replication, surrender, and disappearance. Carrellee joins him on the album’s duet, Feel This Flame Unfold, extending a collaboration that will continue throughout the upcoming North American and European tours. Post-Punk.com spoke with van der Velde about the Nirvana and Björk records that first drew him toward songwriting, growing up beyond Drenthe’s blues and metal scenes, the growth of the Dutch wave underground, and Grauzone’s international role. He also discusses the unlikely longevity of Bragolin’s earliest songs, the backlash surrounding the video for Not All Are Real, the visual rules that keep faces concealed, the band’s first North American tour, and his ambition to develop concept albums and, perhaps one day, a Bragolin film. Bragolin. Photo by Lisanne Lentink Edwin, what were the first records or artists that seized your imagination growing up, and when did listening turn into the desire to write and perform your own music? When I was a kid, I mostly listened to local radio before I got a few pop music cassettes in the early ’90s, which were full of Eurodance. I didn’t care much about music until I discovered alternative music in my mid-teens. Nirvana and Björk were the artists who opened up that world for me. I was fascinated by what felt like the purity of Nirvana’s music, while Björk showed me how unconventional and unique an artist could be. Nevermind, Unplugged, and Post were the first three albums I owned. For most of those later teenage years, I listened almost exclusively to Nirvana. That inspired me to buy a guitar and start writing songs. You can still hear Nirvana’s influence beneath the surface in my music, in the song structures, the desire to write catchy melodies, and even in the way I often add the lyrics later in the songwriting process. Which books and writers had the strongest effect on you during those formative years? Were there particular novels that shaped Bragolin’s fascination with isolation, dread, and the uncanny? I’ve never been much of a reader. I have difficulty focusing on black letters on a white page. Visuals are what draw my attention. While I’m trying to translate the words into images, my mind often drifts off into its own story. I suddenly realize I’m no longer reading the text and have to go back and start again. It’s rare that I truly enjoy reading. So films have had a much bigger influence on me. It’s a shame, because all my life I’ve heard people say that books are so much more interesting than the films. Bragolin’s music and videos seem to draw from post-apocalyptic and horror cinema, including Gothic and folk horror, science-fiction paranoia, body horror, and cosmic horror. Which films first opened those worlds to you, and what do you tend to take from them—the setting, pacing, imagery, or emotional psychology? As a teenager, I was a big fan of the Terminator and Predator films. My dad has always loved action movies, so I grew up watching a lot of the classics with him. Later on, I discovered arthouse cinema, which gradually introduced me to folk horror. The Village (2004) and The Witch (2015) are great examples of the kind of settings and atmosphere I enjoy. I’m especially drawn to the vulnerability of the main character and the mystery and ambiguity of whatever they’re up against. I like to focus on that tension in my lyrics instead of the gore, although I enjoy those films as well. How did growing up in the Netherlands shape your musical imagination? Are there aspects of the Dutch landscape, culture, or temperament that have found their way into Bragolin? I don’t think growing up in the Netherlands consciously shaped Bragolin very much. I grew up in the province of Drenthe, where blues and metal were pretty much the only music scenes around. That made me realize quite early on that I had to look elsewhere to find like-minded people. Having said that, Dutch folklore is something I’d love to explore one day. I think it could make a great concept album. How would you describe the Dutch post-punk and darkwave scene today? Does it possess a character distinct from the scenes you have encountered elsewhere in Europe and Latin America? The Dutch wave scene has improved enormously over the last decade. It’s still a smaller and somewhat more reserved scene compared to our neighbouring countries, but it’s definitely moving in the right direction. Thanks to the hard work of promoters, musicians, and a new generation of fans, the scene has become much more hopeful than it was ten years ago. With festivals like Grauzone, Wavefest, and Momentum, we now have events of a high international standard. Artists like Adam Tristar, Raderkraft, Lifeless Past, De Ambassade, Silent Runners, Camy Huot, Pol, and many more are finding international success. A decade ago, the Dutch wave scene was mostly known internationally because Clan of Xymox came from here. Now there’s a much broader and healthier scene. Bragolin performed at Grauzone in The Hague earlier this year. What was that experience like, and what role has Grauzone played in connecting the Dutch underground with the wider international post-punk community? This year marked our second appearance at Grauzone. We were only announced as a last-minute replacement three days before the festival, so it was great to see such an enthusiastic response from the audience. What I enjoy most about Grauzone is seeing people from both the Dutch and international wave scene together, alongside visitors from outside the scene. Grauzone has made the genre much more accessible to people who might never have considered going to a post-punk or darkwave festival before. I think that’s played a huge role in helping the scene grow in the Netherlands and in connecting the Dutch underground with the wider international community. Can you take us back to the creation of “Into Those Woods”? Which arrived first: the baritone melody, the repeating organ hook, the rhythm, or those images of the manor, the swing, and the mysterious book? This is an interesting question because it was actually the very first Bragolin song I wrote. It all started with that guitar riff I originally had in mind for my other project, Zwarte Poëzie, in early 2013. In mid-2013, I bought a Bass VI, and when I tried the riff on that instrument, everything suddenly clicked. That Bass VI sound became the foundation of Bragolin when I decided to start it as a second project later that year. Because most of Zwarte Poëzie’s lyrics had been about my personal life, I wanted Bragolin to explore different themes. After watching The Evil Dead, I wrote the lyrics inspired by the film. Around that time I was also a big fan of the band The Organ and wanted to use an organ sound instead of relying mainly on synths like many darkwave bands. That became another defining element of Bragolin’s sound. “Into Those Woods” has surpassed fourteen million streams and become a modern darkwave classic. When did you first realize the song had taken on a life beyond the debut album, and how has your relationship with it changed since 2018? I started Bragolin without any expectations. We were just focused on making music the way we wanted to and making it as good as possible. Being in Zwarte Poëzie for eight years had taught me that success was difficult to achieve, although we did have some success with De Laatste Dagen as a minor dancefloor hit while I was working on the first Bragolin album. I assumed “Into Those Woods” might be too catchy and sound too clean for the goth scene, but fortunately I was wrong. The interesting thing is that the song’s reach kept growing year after year. Every year it felt like, “Okay, we’ve probably reached the ceiling now,” but it kept growing. What’s even more surprising is that “This Grotesque Dance” suddenly became a TikTok hit this winter, despite already being out there for seven years. Over the past year, it even surpassed “Into Those Woods” as our most streamed song. I’m very happy that our fans have embraced the new album just as much, and that Bragolin has grown beyond that one song. When we play live, it sometimes feels like we’ve already had a great show and then there’s that moment of, “Oh wait, we still have this song to come.” When you begin writing a Bragolin song now, what form does the first idea usually take? Could you walk us through the process of developing that fragment into a finished arrangement? For me, having a strong hook on top of a danceable beat and bassline is the foundation. I usually put on a drumbeat and play my Bass VI for hours until I find a riff that I like. I then record it and put it aside for weeks or even months. Listening back to a collection of these basic ideas later makes it easier to distinguish which ones have the most potential. After choosing the strongest one, I develop the riff into a song, often starting by humming vocal lines and eventually replacing those with rough lyrics. I then develop those lyrics into a story, which can be inspired by films I’ve recently watched. After that, I layer the song with additional instruments and sound recordings. On the latest album, I put more focus on that layering process than on the first two albums. For the next album, I would like to focus more on having strong foundations again, similar to the approach I took on the first album. “I Run and Hide” sounds heavily guitar-driven, yet its entire instrumental body was constructed from layered Clavinets. How did you record and process those layers, and what did that self-imposed limitation allow you to discover? After the second album, I bought a bunch of new instruments to embrace creativity. One of them was a small electric piano with different sounds built into it. For this song, I ran it through my Bass VI setup, which is why it doesn’t sound too far removed from the way the Bass VI normally sounds. Because it was a piano sound, I wanted to arrange it as if it could actually be played as a piano piece, with a low bass melody and multiple high melodies. I wanted it to feel like one instrument was playing the whole piece. It showed me that by limiting myself to one sound, I could still create a full arrangement with its own character. I Don’t Like What It Does to Me also incorporates field recordings, synthetic ocean textures, waterphones, and other unconventional sources. Could you identify a few moments where those sounds appear and explain how you manipulated them? For this album, I wanted it to have a more cinematic feel. One of the instruments I started using was the waterphone, which is often used in film scores and sound effects. It appears at various moments throughout the album, but it is especially noticeable at the beginning of the title track and This Presence Like a Breeze. This cinematic approach is also why I used a string section at the beginning of “Not All Are Real” to somewhat recreate the feeling of the opening of The Thing (2011), which is a prequel to the classic 1982 film. There are also two songs with ocean-inspired sounds: “Tar With Salt Foam” and “I Salute You Ancient Ocean”. For both songs, I created the sound of ocean waves with my Korg MS-20 by using synthesis rather than recordings of actual waves, while the seagulls were recorded as field recordings. I then processed and layered these sounds into the arrangements to create the atmosphere I was looking for. Where do your lyrics usually begin—with a personal experience, an image, a line from a book, or a scene from a film? How do you turn an outside reference into something that carries your own emotional meaning? It usually starts with a hummed vocal line, and then I look for words that fit the sounds and rhythm of that melody. From there, a few words become the basis of the lyrics. While watching films, I write down how I experience them visually and emotionally from the perspective of the protagonist. But I don’t want to create a direct interpretation of the film. It is more a starting point for my own lyrics, and often I turn it into my own story rather than sticking to the original inspiration. Which artists working in the current post-punk, darkwave, or experimental underground are exciting you most at the moment? Are there any Dutch acts in particular that you believe deserve a much wider audience? My listening has always been broader than just post-punk and darkwave, but from time to time I return to these genres, and there are still artists within the scene that I find very inspiring. I was pleasantly surprised by Carrellee’s music when she joined our record label, Young & Cold Records, with her self-titled 2025 album. I ended up listening to that album on repeat, which led to us getting in contact, collaborating on songs, and working together on upcoming tours. Other artists within our genre that I’ve been enjoying lately are Grundeis, The Woken Trees, The Soft Moon, Boy Harsher, Dead Man’s Bones, and Murder by Death. However, I have mainly been listening to a lot of 60s music, from Ennio Morricone and The Shadows to Nancy Sinatra and Roy Orbison. It is still often dark and melancholic music, and I think I know what elements to take from other genres and what to leave behind when creating my own music. Bragolin’s videos have become an important extension of the songs, from the manor and woodland imagery of “Into Those Woods” to the nocturnal pursuit through streets and cornfields in “I Run and Hide.” How closely involved are you in developing those concepts, and what do you look for in a director? I usually create at least one music video per album myself. For the others, when looking for a director or editor, the most important thing is that they understand the music, respect our visual identity, and have a fitting portfolio. With the new album, I wanted to create more original footage instead of reusing existing material as on previous albums. My role is mainly setting guidelines, such as avoiding showing faces clearly in our visual content. We call this anonymity. This connects with our album covers, which are all portraits shot from behind, and our lyrics, where we also leave room for interpretation rather than explaining everything too clearly. I Run and Hide was made by two very talented film students, Maria Gaedcke and Jonathan Eder. It was our first time working with a larger production. My idea was to combine the inspiration for the song, the film It Follows (2014), with the new album cover’s figure in the nightgown, while taking the opposite approach to the film by not showing the antagonist explicitly. The video for “Feel This Flame Unfold” was created by State of Poison, who had caught our attention with several great animated productions. Animation offered a chance to explore another style, and I’m really happy with how all the videos turned out. For “Not All Are Real,” you connected The Thing and Invasion of the Body Snatchers with contemporary anxiety about artificial replication, using intentionally unnatural AI-generated imagery. What creative and ethical boundaries did you establish for that video, and did the response to it alter your view of the technology? Even though it received quite a lot of negative responses, I still think the concept I wanted to create was only possible in this way. The video is about artificial replication, so using AI-generated imagery became part of the concept itself rather than just a production tool. Filming people in public without their consent would have raised ethical concerns. Emptying the streets of major cities around the world to create a film set and hiring hundreds of actors simply isn’t realistic within the budget of an independent band. Animation, on the other hand, wouldn’t have captured the unsettling feeling of cloned humans that I was looking for. The only real alternative would have been to abandon the concept and make a completely different video. I also found it interesting that we’d previously used existing footage in our videos, which raises ethical questions of its own, yet that never received the same criticism. That said, the reaction was enough for me to decide: never again. Bragolin will embark on its first North American tour this fall. What are you most looking forward to experiencing on this run, and when you look beyond it, where would you like to take Bragolin next—musically, visually, and geographically? We have had a following in North America for a long time, and the requests for us to come over have gone unanswered for many years. I’m mainly looking forward to finally meeting those fans who have been following us from the beginning and hopefully giving them the show they’ve been waiting for. Looking beyond this tour, I’d like Bragolin to remain a constant by continuing to make albums for many years to come. I’d also love to explore the possibility of creating concept albums, which is an element from the past I’d like to bring back to the present, and combine that with even more visual storytelling, perhaps one day creating our own dedicated film. Geographically, there are still plenty of places we haven’t visited. In early 2027, we’re planning a West Coast tour and a return to Latin America.§ Listen to I Don’t Like What It Does To Me below and order the album here. I Don’t Like What It Does To Me by Bragolin Looking towards the horizon, Edwin Van der Velde hopes to expand Bragolin through future concept albums and, eventually, a film devoted to the project’s visual world. Yet, the immediate priority is Bragolin’s first North American tour. Van der Velde and synth player Edwin Daatselaar will take the band on the road alongside Carrellee for the thirty-date North American Hope Tour, beginning September 3 at X-Ray Arcade in the Milwaukee area. Bragolin has maintained a substantial North American audience for years, yet these will be the duo’s first performances on the continent. The route continues through the Midwest, Ontario and Quebec, the Northeast, the South, and Texas before ending October 11 in Tulsa. Bragolin then returns to Europe for dates beginning October 31 in Utrecht and running through December 19 in Brussels, followed by São Paulo and Santiago in February 2027. A separate West Coast tour is also being planned for early 2027, though its dates have yet to be announced. The schedule reflects the unusual way Bragolin’s audience has grown. Into Those Woods accumulated listeners steadily until it passed ten million streams, while This Grotesque Dance found a new audience through TikTok seven years after its release and eventually became Bragolin’s most-streamed song. Those songs reached North America well before the band could follow them. After years of requests from listeners across the continent, van der Velde and Daatselaar will finally meet that audience in person this fall. items.body: Magic Wands released the single “Diamond Rain” on August 14, 2026 through Metropolis Records. The Los Angeles duo of vocalists and guitarists Dexy and Chris Valentine mix dream-pop with shoegaze, post-punk and goth, and the track is the first to be lifted from a new Magic Wands album due in early 2027. It is out digitally, with a self-made video posted to the band’s YouTube channel the same day. Diamond Rain by Magic Wands What Magic Wands say about ‘Diamond Rain’ The duo describe the song as deliberately open rather than fixed: “the song doesn’t have one fixed meaning. To us, it’s about moving toward the light, finding beauty after darkness and allowing people to discover their own meaning within it.” They made the accompanying video themselves and explain how the look was built: “using old cameras, lights and mirrors to create textures and effects that give it a dreamlike feeling.” “Diamond Rain” streams and downloads through Bandcamp and the usual digital services. No physical edition has been announced, and the duo have not named the 2027 album or given it a date. ‘Diamond Rain’ follows two EPs and a Peter Murphy remix The single closes an unusually busy eighteen months. The album “Cascades” arrived on October 24, 2025, trailed by the double single “Time To Dream” backed with “Armour (River Remix by Lost Signal)” the previous month. A Delerium remix of “Moonshadow” followed on March 13, 2026. Two EPs came after that. The “Wishing Well” EP, six songs issued on April 24, 2026, was preceded by its title track in February and by “Sacred Mirrors”, a January 2026 collaboration with John Ashton of The Psychedelic Furs. The six-track “Remixes” EP landed on June 12, 2026 and reworked material from “Cascades”. In between, the pair remixed Peter Murphy; Side-Line covered that single when Peter Murphy released “Swoon (Magic Wands Remix)” on May 29, 2026. About Magic Wands Magic Wands formed in Nashville in 2008 around Dexy and Chris Valentine, who share vocals and guitars, and later moved to Los Angeles. Metropolis Records describes their sound as heavily textured guitars, droning synths and ethereal vocals. The duo have released through Metropolis for over a decade. Side-Line first covered them in April 2022 around the single “Fortune”, then the single “Time” in May 2023 and the remix album and tour that August. The album “Switch” followed in 2023 and was reviewed here that September. “Cascades” came in October 2025 and drew the run of singles, remixes and EPs that “Diamond Rain” now brings to a close, with the next album set for early 2027.

items.body: ITCH have made a debut record called “House of Ghosts” available to stream on Escape.ai, a distribution platform and creator marketplace for generative AI and game-technology work founded by John Gaeta, an American visual effects designer, inventor, and creative director. The project describes the album like this: “House of Ghosts is a dark, alternative journey through memory, identity, loss, and the parts of ourselves that refuse to disappear. Split between ANIMUS and ANIMA, the album explores masculine and feminine inner worlds as two haunted sides of the same soul.” Ten tracks are posted with official audio and full lyrics: “Somewhere to Hide“, “Two”, “Temp”, “Throne”, “Alone”, “Time”, “Wrong”, “Son”, “Keep Your Roots” and “Void”. The lyrics deal with grief and absence (“Time takes everything”), sibling violence (“There were two. Then there was one”), suppressed anger (“It’s not anger, it’s a temperature”) and isolation (“I’m alone in my skin”). No writer, performer, producer or engineer is named against any of them. Due to the ban on AI music on several platforms, the album will probably only be available on Escape.ai for the moment being. About Escape.ai Escape.ai is a next-generation entertainment streaming and content distribution platform dedicated to pioneering the future of digital storytelling. Founded by Academy Award-winning visual effects designer John Gaeta (The Matrix), the platform serves as a curated, premium showcase for “Neo Cinema” and “Neo Play”. Unlike open social media feeds where AI content is frequently lost in the noise, Escape.ai positions itself as a prestige destination for premium, human-authored stories that are super-amplified by technology. The network champions independent creators, offering them a way to scale their original intellectual property and achieve blockbuster-level world-building without relying on traditional, rigid Hollywood studio pipelines. The network is actively streaming across major platforms like Roku and The Roku Channel, Amazon Fire TV, Samsung Smart TVs, and LG TVs, with expansion onto Apple TV and PC environments.

items.body: Elsieanne Caplette, singer and composer of Montreal trip-hop duo Elsiane, announced on August 12, 2026 that she has begun a solo project separate from the band. She made the announcement in a message to subscribers of the Elsiane Bandcamp page, and used the same message to confirm that Elsiane are planning tour dates for 2027. No title, release date, format or label has been named for the solo material. What Elsieanne Caplette has confirmed so far Caplette said she has been working on the project privately and is holding the details back for now: “Lately, I’ve been quietly working on something that’s entirely my own. I’m beginning a new solo chapter. I’m not quite ready to reveal everything yet, but I can tell you that this project feels deeply personal and unlike anything I’ve shared before.” She pointed readers to a new mailing list at elsieannecaplette.com for the first announcements. Nothing further about the solo work is public: no title, no release date, no format, no label, no collaborators and no production credits. Her bandmate Stephane Sotto is not mentioned in the message, and Caplette does not say whether the solo project affects Elsiane. Elsiane tour dates are planned for 2027 The message closed with the band’s own plans. Caplette wrote: “And for everyone wondering, yes… Elsiane is planning some tour dates next year and some surprises. We’ll be sharing more details this fall.” No cities, venues, countries or on-sale dates are confirmed, and the duo have not said whether the run supports new Elsiane material. The wording places the full announcement in autumn 2026. Elsiane have been signalling a return to the road for some time. Caplette told Canadian Beats in September 2023, ahead of the self-titled album, that the duo were “planning to have some shows for next year” and were hoping to book tour dates. Those dates did not follow, which makes the 2027 window the first firm timeframe the band have given since. The most recent Elsiane release is the self-titled album “Elsiane”, issued on October 3, 2023 through Labratoryband Inc. and produced by David Bottrill. Side-Line covered it when the duo prepped an October release for the all new album, simply titled “Elsiane”. Seven tracks: “Traces of the Heart”, “Tu Mirada”, “Sinai”, “Loneliness”, “Soul Travelling”, “Fading Star” and “Under Aghast”. Elsiane by E L S I A N E About Elsiane Elsieanne Caplette was born in Montmagny, Quebec, and trained in classical music at the Lima Conservatory in Peru; Wikipedia records that she grew up in Peru, sang in a group there and moved to Montreal in 1999. There she met Stephane Sotto, a self-taught drummer born in Montreal. The two began working together in 2000 and named the project by joining the first four letters of her first name to the last three of his. Their music pulls on jazz, downtempo, rock, classical, electronic and world music, and they cite the trip-hop of Massive Attack and Portishead alongside Bjork, Kate Bush and Peter Gabriel. The debut album “Hybrid” arrived on May 1, 2007 on Vega, with Nettwerk issuing it in the United States the following year. Live work followed, including tours with Delerium and Beast, and a contribution to the soundtrack for Quebec City’s 400th anniversary alongside Cirque du Soleil and Booka Shade. On stage the line-up has included Jeff Feldman on bass and keyboards and Philippe Look on guitar and keyboards. The self-produced second album “Mechanics of Emotion” followed on April 10, 2012 on Labratoryband Inc., trailed by the single and video “Underhelped”, and drew more openly on acoustic and traditional instruments. A third album, “Death of the Artist”, came out independently in 2017 after the duo ran into difficulties with the music industry, and in 2018 they worked with the writer Rich Shapero on “Rin, Tongue and Dorner”. Side-Line has tracked the band across that stretch, covering the 2016 surprise single “Unstable” and the 2020 return single “Sinai”. Sotto’s father died in 2018 and the pair started writing the next record in his memory, with production beginning in July 2019 under Bottrill. “Tu Mirada”, released in October 2022 and sung in Spanish, drew on Caplette’s Peruvian upbringing. The finished album added guest players including Pedro Eustache, Trey Gunn of King Crimson, Tony Grey and Caroline Plante, and came out on October 3, 2023. It remains the duo’s last release, and Caplette’s solo announcement is the first news from either member since.

The London electronic and industrial group posted the video to their own Portion Control VMAG channel. Portion Control rebuild ‘Refugee’ as ‘Displaced Hybrid Refugee’ “Displaced Hybrid R
items.body: Portion Control released a video for “Displaced Hybrid Refugee” on August 14, 2026, the same day their first archival box set, “1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge…”, arrived on Artoffact Records as a 4xCD set, a digital edition and a limited red vinyl LP. The London electronic and industrial group posted the video to their own Portion Control VMAG channel. Portion Control rebuild ‘Refugee’ as ‘Displaced Hybrid Refugee’ “Displaced Hybrid Refugee” sits at track 56 of the 77-track set and reworks “Refugee”, originally on the 1984 album “..Step Forward”. The band explain where the footage came from rather than what the song means: “This song is a rework of ‘Refugee’ and the video is built from the visuals used whenever we play it live.” It is the second rebuild of that song to surface from the project. Rhys Fulber of Front Line Assembly produced “Refugee (Rhys Fulber Rebuild)”, the first preview issued when the box set was announced. What the ‘Hit The Pulse to Purge’ box set collects The set gathers the 1983 mini-LP “Hit The Pulse”, the albums “..Step Forward” (1984) and “Psycho Bod Saves The World” (1986), the 12-inch singles “The Great Divide”, “Go-Talk” and “Raise The Pulse”, and the “Purge” EP (1986), plus B-sides, compilation tracks, rarities, remixes, demos and two concert recordings from 1984 and 1985. Paul Lavigne remastered all 77 tracks at Kontrast Mastering. Sixteen are previously unreleased and a further twelve appear on CD and digitally for the first time. The 4xCD edition comes in a five-panel ecopak with a 24-page booklet of archive photos, designed by Stefan Alt of ant-zen. The red vinyl LP carries ten tracks. 1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge… by portion control Side-Line covered the set when Artoffact announced the box set “1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge…” in June. Two further previews followed over the summer: the live recording “Tex-Mex”, taped at Dolce Vita in Lausanne in December 1985, and the demo “H.O.T. Matter” from the “Psycho Bod Saves The World” period. All three earlier tracks are on the box set alongside “Displaced Hybrid Refugee”. The 4xCD box, the LP, the digital edition and a run of six vinyl test pressings are sold through Bandcamp. The set is also on Spotify, Apple Music and Amazon Music, with physical copies handled in the UK by Lexer Music. Portion Control live dates October 24, 2026 – Zwickau, Germany – Elektrisch Festival July 1-4, 2027 – Canterbury, United Kingdom – Shadowlands About Portion Control Portion Control formed in South London in 1979 around Dean Piavani, Ian Sharp and John Whybrew. The group built a minimal, rhythm-led sound from sequenced synthesisers, drum machines, early samplers and clipped vocals, and issued a run of cassettes before their first vinyl album, “I Staggered Mentally”, in 1982. The mini-LP “Hit The Pulse” followed in 1983 and “..Step Forward” in 1984, the year they toured with Depeche Mode. “Psycho Bod Saves The World” closed the period in 1986. Their records from these years are cited as an influence on Nitzer Ebb, Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly, Nine Inch Nails and Orbital. The band stopped in the late 1980s and returned in 2004 with “Wellcome”, followed by “Filthy White Guy” (2006) and “Pure Form” (2012). Side-Line spoke to them in 2020 in an interview with Portion Control, and covered the 2022 reissue of the “Dissolve” material after the original run was pressed on self-destroying discs. Three “SEED” EPs appeared between 2020 and 2025, the last of them, “SEED EP3.1”, marking the point where Portion Control joined Artoffact in late 2025. “1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge…” is the first box set in the reissue programme that deal set up, and “Displaced Hybrid Refugee” is the track the band chose to mark its release.

items.body: Swedish electro artist EMMON released “Relics (Agent Side Grinder Remix)” on 14 August 2026 through Icons Creating Evil Art. The track is the third remix issued ahead of “ICONMIXED”, a remix album scheduled for 23 October 2026. Jimmy Monell produced and mixed the new version, Hans Olsson mastered it, and Emma Nylén is credited as writer. The original “Relics” is the eighth track on “ICON“, the album EMMON released on 17 October 2025 with Emanuel Åström as guestvocalist. Agent Side Grinder move it off its EBM footing and into house tempo, adding LinnDrum programming, a Euro-disco riff and acid basslines. Johan Lange of Agent Side Grinder set out what the duo changed: “Had a great time remixing my dear friend Emmon (and a certain obscure guest singer). I took the EBM-driven original and pushed it in a more ’90s house direction, with LinnDrum, a Euro disco riff and plenty of acid basslines.” Two reworkings of “Speak to Me” preceded it, one by SIIE and one by Copenhagen trio The Foreign Resort. “ICONMIXED” reworks material from “ICON” across a wider set of collaborators. Icons Creating Evil Art issued an official video for the original “Relics” the same day. Niklas Kärreskog directed it, with Tyko Lann Lundin as editing assistant and Joakim Kärreskog on technical resources. Kärreskog set out his reference points in the video credits: “Relics could easily be part of the soundtrack to a film adaptation of William Gibson’s Neuromancer. That’s why I aimed for a cyberpunk aesthetic inspired by Ridley Scott’s Alien (1979) and Shinya Tsukamoto’s Tetsuo (1989). To achieve this, the video was processed through a CRT television and many metres of cable.” EMMON has run this pattern before. “RECON” arrived in 2022 and drew a full companion remix record a year later; “ICONMIXED” applies the same treatment to the newer album. About EMMON EMMON is the solo project of Swedish artist and producer Emma Nylén, based in Stockholm and signed to Icons Creating Evil Art. Her earlier catalogue runs from “The Art and The Evil” and “Closet Wanderings” through “Nomme”, “AON” and “Under Construction”, built on hard synth basslines, clipped vocals and melodic electro structures. “RECON” followed on 7 October 2022 and reopened that catalogue after an extended gap. Its eleven tracks include “Machines”, “Like A Drum” and “Purebloods”, a duet with Agent Side Grinder vocalist Emanuel Åström that set up the working relationship behind the current remix. On 6 October 2023 EMMON issued “RECONMIXED”, a thirteen-track companion that handed “Machines”, “Reconstruction”, “Purebloods” and others to Ultra Sunn, Tobias Bernstrup, Sex Kino, Harlem, Fred White, Maschine Brennt, Majestoluxe, ZackZackZack, Potochkine and Livmødr. The “XCEPTION” EP came next, then “ICON” on 17 October 2025, a ten-track album covering “Neon Brown”, “Decisions”, “Shades of Blue”, “Cold Within”, “No Mans Land”, “Speak to Me”, “Blood on the Ceiling feat. Majestoluxe”, “Relics”, “DARK” and “Slow Running”. Icons Creating Evil Art issued it on vinyl, CD and digital. Side-Line covered that release and published an EMMON interview in February 2026. The rollout toward “ICONMIXED” started with SIIE and The Foreign Resort on “Speak to Me” and continues with Agent Side Grinder on “Relics”. The album is due on 23 October 2026.

items.body: London-based queer alt-metal artist Ray Noir releases “Gothstar” on 13 August 2026, a rave-metal single featuring New York alternative artist Danny Blu. The track is the final single ahead of Ray Noir’s second EP, also titled “Gothstar,” scheduled for 17 September 2026. A label, catalogue number and full tracklist for the EP have not been confirmed. Ray Noir “Gothstar” EP release date and earlier singles The “Gothstar” EP is scheduled for 17 September 2026 and follows three 2026 singles building up to the EP release. “Label Whxre” arrived on 2 April 2026, the release on which Kerrang! reported the EP as a “rave meets metalcore” record. “Black” followed on 14 May 2026, produced by Jon Cass and written with Tom Saint. “Boys” was issued as the third single. KALTBLUT magazine reported in April 2026 that the EP would include a collaboration with Danny Blu without naming the track, and now the 13 August release confirms that collaboration as the title track. “Gothstar” The single combines techno, metalcore and rave production. Promotional material for the release describes the track as moving from the Berlin club Berghain “straight into the mosh pit,” and frames its themes as goth glamour, queer confidence and self-expression. “Gothstar” is also the name of the character at the centre of the EP, and the EP’s title track. Ray Noir released an official music video with the single. Both artists of course appropriately in black leather 😉 “Gothstar” release party in London Ray Noir will host a free release party at Slim Jim’s Liquor Store in London on 19 September 2026. Tickets are listed via DICE. About Ray Noir Ray Noir is a queer alternative artist based in London. According to his official biography, his background is in Oslo’s black-metal underground, and his sound combines metal guitars with electronic club production. He began releasing solo material with the single “Double Trouble” in 2014 and has since worked with a range of underground collaborators. His 2024 mixtape “Scorpio” reached the top five of the German Alternative Charts according to his official biography, and drew coverage from Kerrang! and BBC Radio 1. The 2025 EP “Against the Machine” followed and featured guitarist Steve Stevens. In 2026 he released “Temptation” and “Breathe,” then opened the “Gothstar” campaign with “Label Whxre,” “Black” and “Boys.” Live, his official biography lists sold-out headline shows in London and Oslo, multiple UK tours, performances in Tokyo and at Flow Festival in Finland and Resistanz Festival in the UK, and support slots for Combichrist and Die Krupps. His work in fashion, including with Marc Jacobs and Vivienne Westwood, was cited by KALTBLUT magazine as an influence on “Label Whxre.” No Wikipedia article for Ray Noir surfaced during verification, and Discogs did not return a matching profile, so discography formats and catalogue numbers could not be cross-checked. About Danny Blu Danny Blu is an alternative artist based in New York and the former frontman of Echo Black. He relaunched his solo project with the single “Bubble” in 2019 and released the EPs “The Pale Horse” and “Molotov” in 2021. “Gothstar” is his first confirmed recorded collaboration with Ray Noir.

items.body: Los Angeles band Bizou will release the six-track EP “Widow” on Moonboot Records on 25 September 2026. The band recorded, mixed and mastered the EP at The Cave Studio in Los Angeles. “Death Mag” is the track already streaming with the digital pre-order. Bizou put six tracks on ‘Widow’, recorded at The Cave Studio “Widow” runs “Deep REM”, “Widow”, “No One Can Have You”, “Death Mag”, “Ahead” and “Losing My Memory”. “Death Mag” runs 4:20. The line-up on the EP is Marisa Prietto on lead vocals, synth, bass and guitar, Josiah Mazzaschi on guitar, synth, programming and backing vocals, Nicole Fiorentino on bass and backing vocals, and Nicki Nevlin on guitar. Digital pre-orders are open on Bandcamp, with the download offered in 24-bit/44.1kHz. A “Widow” listening party is listed for 24 September 2026, the day before release. The EP is Bizou’s first new music since the single “Ursula” in October 2023. It is also their first release on Moonboot Records; the band issued their 2018 to 2021 records themselves. Widow by Bizou About Bizou Bizou formed in Los Angeles in 2017 around lead vocalist Marisa Prietto, guitarist and producer Josiah Mazzaschi, bassist Nicole Fiorentino and guitarist Nicki Nevlin. Prietto had previously sung with Wax Idols and Glaare, Mazzaschi came from Light FM, and Fiorentino had played bass with Smashing Pumpkins and Veruca Salt. The band describe their sound on Bandcamp as “driving post-punk bass + wall of sheeny shoegaze guitars + shifting scales of synths + the propulsive rhythms of darkwave […] all fused together with dreamy vocals”, naming Curve, Cranes, Garbage and PJ Harvey as reference points. Bizou opened with the single “Superstition” on 25 October 2018. The self-titled EP “Bizou” followed on 1 March 2019 on cassette and digital, then the EP “stilllifeburning” on 10 April 2020. The nine-track debut album “Tragic Lover” arrived on 4 June 2021, also recorded at The Cave Studio. Two singles closed that phase: an LCD Soundsystem cover, “Tribulations”, on 24 July 2023, and “Ursula” on 20 October 2023. Prietto and Mazzaschi reconvened at The Cave Studio in the summer of 2025. Those sessions produced “Widow”, which now brings Bizou back after nearly three years without a release.

items.body: Pittsburgh industrial project ShadowMouth and Cleveland vocal trio The Elder Goths released the double single “The Promise of Alchemy/The Death of Chemistry” on 12 August 2026 through Death of the Party Records. The two tracks are the final preview of ShadowMouth’s debut album “Modern Alchemy”, due in autumn 2026. How ShadowMouth and The Elder Goths built the two tracks Rick Polo and Brooks Farris wrote and performed the music. The Elder Goths, made up of Cassandra Bishop, Lauren O’Janpa and Gina Schultz, sing on both sides. Bishop wrote the lyrics for “The Promise of Alchemy”, which runs 2:29, and Schultz wrote the lyrics for “The Death of Chemistry”, which runs 2:24. Farris produced, engineered and mastered the pair at Electric Fox Studios. Polo had not met the three singers before he asked them to record, and he describes the approach as a gamble that changed the shape of the release. “These songs were the result of me taking a shot in the dark and reaching out The Elder Goths group, who I had never met before, and asked if they would provide some of the striking beautifully haunting harmonies that are immediately apparent when first hearing their work,” Polo stated. “But it turned out to be so much more than I could have imagined. The end result was an intense and and really heartfelt delivery which absolutely blew me away. This collaboration felt too important not to highlight. So we decided to release this a single ahead of the record.” The double single is available on Bandcamp. The Promise of Alchemy/The Death of Chemistry by ShadowMouth & The Elder Goths About ShadowMouth ShadowMouth formed in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania in 2023 as the project of songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Rick Polo, who also plays in Baroque Monody and Heck Vektor. Producer and drummer Brooks Farris of Electric Fox Studios completes the working pair. The project opened with the double single “Poison Nostalgia/Twenty Four Hours” on 4 October 2024, with Dombroski guesting on “Poison Nostalgia”. The debut EP “Purification By Fire” followed on 22 November 2024. Four singles came next: “False (Prophets) Profits” on 20 January 2025, “Your Words, Not Mine” on 21 May 2025, “We Are Sentient” on 1 August 2025 and “DOOM SCROLLERS vs HOLY ROLLERS” on 29 October 2025. The Elder Goths formed in 2024 in Cleveland, Ohio, after Cassandra Bishop, Lauren O’Janpa and Gina Schultz met through the city’s underground scene. “The Promise of Alchemy/The Death of Chemistry” is their first recorded appearance with ShadowMouth. With the twin tracks out, ShadowMouth close a run of seven releases in under two years and move to “Modern Alchemy”, the project’s first album.

items.body: Oxford band Shaven Primates released the four-track EP “Kill The Algorithm” on TAD Records on 31 July 2026. The EP runs 17 minutes and 53 seconds. What Shaven Primates address on ‘Kill The Algorithm’ The EP opens with “Saviour” (4:26), then moves through “Pioneer Way” (3:30) and “Feed” (4:28) before the title track “Kill The Algorithm” (5:28). Across the four songs the band take on dependency, tabloid conditioning, grievance politics and the mechanics of social media. “Pioneer Way” sets its argument in a Britain of workplace exhaustion and scapegoating, with the line “Commonplace everyday wreck of the UK”. The title track turns on the repeated command of its own name. Shaven Primates describe themselves on Bandcamp as “a 5-piece dark-wave, art-rock, post-punk band that seeks to push the boundaries of the genre”, adding that their “music is a narrative of human emotion and experience; fear, love and anger resonate through the orchestration, giving a deeply cathartic release”. “Kill The Algorithm” is on Spotify. The band’s Bandcamp page currently lists their three earlier releases only, so the EP cannot be bought there yet. About Shaven Primates Shaven Primates are based in Oxford, UK, and mix darkwave, art-rock and post-punk with harder guitar work. The band’s own summary of that mix is short: their music is “a narrative of human emotion and experience”. Their Bandcamp discography begins with “Child Of Dirt” on 26 November 2021, followed by “Birds Aren’t Real” on 28 July 2023 and “Chasing The Dragon” on 13 December 2024. Neither Discogs nor Wikipedia holds an entry for the band, so the Bandcamp listings remain the clearest record of their releases. “Kill The Algorithm” is their first release since “Chasing The Dragon” in December 2024, and the first to carry the TAD Records imprint.

ATTX · GAIJIN About ATTX ATTX is the dark synthwave project of Attilio Scala, an Italian bassist, multi-instrumentalist, singer and session player, according to his own description. “GAIJIN” is his debut single under the ATTX name, self-released out of Italy and set for release on August 14, 2026. items.body: Hocico‘s debut full-length album, “Odio Bajo El Alma,” turns 29 on 14 August. The Mexican electro-industrial duo released the record on 14 August 1997 through the Mexican label Opción Sónica, with European distribution handled by Out Of Line. ‘Odio Bajo El Alma’ tracklist and credits “Odio Bajo El Alma” was Hocico’s first official release after three self-produced cassette demos – “Misuse, Abuse and Accident” (1993), “Autoagresión Persistente” (1994) and “Triste Desprecio” (1996). The album was produced by Edmundo Navas, with engineering handled by the band alongside Rogelio Gómez. It was issued on CD and cassette in Mexico, later reissued in Germany through Out Of Line and Sub/Mission Records, and reissued again on vinyl by Out Of Line in 2019. The album runs 11 tracks: “Cuando la Maldad Despierta” “Odio en el Alma” “Beings of Relief” “Final Resource” “Hell on Earth” “Gota de Sangre” “Temple of Lies” “Sexo Bajo Testosterona (Frenetik Mix ’96)” “Sad Scorn” “Slow Death” “Face to Face” The record is available to stream via Spotify. According to Wikipedia, “Odio Bajo El Alma” was well received across Europe and the Americas and introduced audiences outside Mexico to a style of electronic music few realized was being made there. Before the album’s release, Hocico had been part of a Mexico City collective called La Corporación, alongside acts such as Cenobita, Ogo, Encefálisis and Deus Ex Machina, that supported and promoted the country’s electronic underground. About Hocico Hocico is a Mexican electro-industrial duo formed in 1993 in Mexico City by cousins Eric García, performing as Erk Aicrag, and Óscar Mayorga, performing as Racso Agroyam. García writes the lyrics and performs vocals, while Mayorga handles programming. Both had experimented with electronic music since their teens, drawing on industrial acts such as Skinny Puppy. Their musical partnership began in 1989 in a group called Niñera Degenerada, and in 1992 the two left that project to form Hocico de Perro, later shortened simply to Hocico. Between 1993 and 1996 the duo self-released three cassette demos before issuing “Odio Bajo El Alma” in 1997 on Opción Sónica with Out Of Line handling European distribution. The end of the decade brought the live album “Los Hijos Del Infierno,” recorded during Hocico’s 1998 European tour, and the studio follow-up “Sangre Hirviente” (1999), which reached number 19 on the CMJ RPM chart in the United States. Hocico played the Zillo festival in Germany and the Euro Rock festival in Belgium in 1999, returned to Germany’s Woodstage festival in 2000 in front of more than 20,000 people, and opened for Rammstein during that band’s 2001 Mexican tour. “Signos De Aberración” followed in 2002, then “Wrack And Ruin” in 2004, after which the band paused new studio material. During the break, García launched his solo project Rabia Sorda and relocated to Leipzig, Germany, while Mayorga remained based in Mexico City. Hocico resumed with “Memorias Atrás” in 2008 and has released an album roughly every two years since: “Tiempos de Furia” (2010), “El Ultimo Minuto” (2012), “Los días caminando en el fuego” (2013), “Ofensor” (2015), “The Spell of the Spider” (2017, which reached number 42 on the German national charts) and “Artificial Extinction” (2019, an album centered on artificial intelligence as a threat to humanity, which peaked at number 30 in Germany). “Hyperviolent” followed in 2022. Side-Line has continued to track the band’s output, including the Hey Tú EP expansion with Prayers and, most recently, the ‘Unseen Horror Scenes’ album, released in May 2026. Twenty-nine years after “Odio Bajo El Alma” introduced the duo to audiences outside Mexico, the album remains the starting point of that catalog.

items.body: 45 Grave released the album “Pick Your Poison” on 14 August 2012 through Frontier Records. The Los Angeles deathrock band’s album turns 14 this year and stood as its first collection of new material in 27 years, following the group’s 1985 breakup after “Sleep in Safety.” Dinah Cancer had reformed 45 Grave in 2004 and rebuilt the lineup several times over the following years. By 2010, the band settled into a configuration of Cancer on vocals, guitarist Frank Agnew (the Adolescents, T.S.O.L.), bassist Brandden Blackwell and drummer Tom Coyne, the lineup that recorded “Pick Your Poison.” The album mixes newly written songs with older, previously unrecorded material and a re-worked version of “Night of the Demons,” for which a video was produced. “Pick Your Poison” contains ten tracks: “Pick Your Poison,” “Night of the Demons,” “Child of Fear,” “Akira,” “A Desert Dream,” “Lucky 214,” “Highway 666,” “Johnny,” “Sorceress” and “Winds of Change.” Frontier Records issued the album on CD and vinyl. Pick Your Poison by 45 Grave About 45 Grave 45 Grave formed in Los Angeles in 1979, growing out of a related project called Vox Pop. The original lineup paired vocalist Dinah Cancer, formerly of Castration Squad, with guitarist Paul B. Cutler, bassist Rob Graves (also known as Rob Ritter, formerly of the Bags and the Gun Club) and drummer Don Bolles of the Germs. The band’s name came from a thrift-store button reading “WE DIG 45 GRAVE.” Alongside Christian Death, 45 Grave is recognized as one of the earliest American gothic rock acts, developing a hybrid of horror punk and gothic rock that came to be known as deathrock. The band’s sole studio album from its original run, “Sleep in Safety,” followed the 1981 single “Black Cross” and built on the earlier fast-paced version of “Partytime,” later slowed down and reworked for the album. A remixed version of “Partytime” appeared on the soundtrack to the 1985 film “The Return of the Living Dead” and became an MTV staple. 45 Grave broke up in 1985. A brief reunion in 1988 produced the live album “Only the Good Die Young,” but the band split again after bassist Rob Graves died in 1990. Dinah Cancer revived 45 Grave in 2004 to mark the band’s 25th anniversary, working through several lineup changes before settling by 2010 on guitarist Frank Agnew, bassist Brandden Blackwell and drummer Tom Coyne. That lineup recorded “Pick Your Poison,” released on Frontier Records on 14 August 2012 as the band’s first collection of new material in 27 years. Guitarist Dylan Thomas, formerly of the Dickies, joined in 2014, and the band has continued to perform since, including a two-day billing at the Cruel World festival in Pasadena in 2022 alongside Bauhaus, Devo, Blondie and Morrissey.

items.body: Swiss pianist and composer Raphael Loher releases “Figuren” on 4 September 2026 through the Lucerne publishing platform Präsens Editionen. The eight-track album comes out digitally and as a limited vinyl edition with artwork and four inlays by Ukrainian-American artist Mykola Haleta. Loher built the record from his own concert recordings rather than from new performances. The tracks are titled “Figuren I” through “Figuren VIII”. Figuren by Raphael Loher How Raphael Loher made ‘Figuren’ The source material is ten intimate concert recordings of Loher performing pieces from “Keemuun”, his debut album. He took those tapes into a residency in the Blenio Valley in Ticino, where he separated out individual melodies, tones and resonances and reassembled them into new configurations. That work produced around thirty initial pieces and also fed his second album, “Hug of Gravity”. He then ran the fragments through a Revox B77 tape machine, shifting their pitch before digitising and reshaping them again. The results range from layered rhythmic microstructures to sparse melodic fragments and long looping passages. Präsens Editionen describes the album as “shaped by intuition, experimentation, and a deliberate distance from his primary instrument – the piano.” Loher expands the piano itself with preparations, effect pedals and tape, which puts the record closer to ambient and electronic composition than to solo piano recital. Raphael Loher live dates 2026 Loher tours Europe from the release date onward: 4 September – Meakusma Festival, Eupen, Belgium (solo) 5 September – Bad Bonn Kilbi, Düdingen, Switzerland (solo, and with Remo Helfenstein) 12 September – Trial & Error Festival, Tribute to Franziska Lingg, Lucerne, Switzerland 30 September – Periscope, Lyon, France (solo) 3 October – Festival Pour Les Oiseaux, Le Havre, France (solo) 30 October – Heiliggeistkapelle, Lucerne, Switzerland (solo) About Raphael Loher Raphael Loher is based in Lucerne, Switzerland, and combines experimental electronic music, ambient and minimalist composition in his work. His debut solo album “Keemuun” came out on three:four records in October 2022. His second, “Hug of Gravity”, followed on the Swiss experimental label Hallow Ground in 2025. He plays in two trios. Baumschule pairs him with guitarist Manuel Troller and drummer Julian Sartorius for long-form improvisation, also released through three:four records. KALI Trio, formed in 2015 with guitarist Urs Müller and drummer Nicolas Stocker, released its third album “The Playful Abstract” in early 2025, and co-wrote the score for “Nemesis”, the documentary by Swiss director Thomas Imbach, alongside Lukas Langenegger. Loher has also played and recorded with Gerry Hemingway of the Anthony Braxton Quartet and with Martina Lussi. He has toured across Europe and appeared at the Montreux Jazz Festival, Willisau Jazz Festival, Cully Jazz Festival, One Of A Million Festival, Jazzfestival Schaffhausen and Unerhört Festival, among others, and his records have been played on BBC 6 Music and BBC Radio 3. “Figuren” is his third album and his first for Präsens Editionen, a Lucerne platform founded in 2011 that publishes magazines, books and records. It moves his catalogue further from live piano documentation and towards tape-based composition.
